questions.q: Explain the three-schema architecture and distinguish logical data independence from physical data independence with one example of each.
questions.model: External (user views), conceptual (whole logical schema) and internal (storage) levels with mappings between them. Physical independence: adding an index or changing file organisation does not change the conceptual schema. Logical independence: adding a column to a table does not change existing external views.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of the DBMS approach over a file system?
opts: Lower cost and overhead for every small application
questions.model: A DBMS adds cost and overhead; for very small, simple applications a file system can be cheaper.

questions.q: True or False: A database schema changes frequently, while the database instance rarely changes.
questions.model: False. The schema (intension) is stable; the instance (extension, the data at a moment) changes with every update.

questions.q: Read the assertion and reason about centralized and client-server architectures and choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: In a three-tier client-server architecture, the client does not connect directly to the database server.
questions.reason: An application server between them runs the business logic and accesses the database on the client's behalf.
questions.model: Both true and R explains A.

questions.q: What is a weak entity type? Explain its identifying relationship and partial key using DEPENDENT of EMPLOYEE as an example.
questions.model: A weak entity has no key of its own; it is identified through an owner entity via an identifying relationship (total participation). DEPENDENT is identified by the owner EMPLOYEE's SSN plus its partial key Dependent_name.

questions.q: Every employee works in exactly one department and a department can have many employees. Which description of WORKS_FOR is correct?
questions.model: Many employees to one department (N:1); every employee must participate (total).

questions.t: Entity Types, Entity Sets, Attributes and Keys
questions.q: Design an ER diagram for the case, identifying entity types, attributes, keys, relationships, cardinality ratios and participation constraints. State any assumptions.
questions.case: A hospital records patients (ID, name, date of birth, phone numbers), doctors (ID, name, specialisation) and wards (number, capacity). A patient is admitted to one ward at a time, may be treated by several doctors, and each doctor treats many patients; each treatment has a date and a diagnosis.
questions.model: Entities PATIENT (PatientID key, Name, DOB, multivalued Phone), DOCTOR (DoctorID key, Name, Specialisation), WARD (WardNo key, Capacity). ADMITTED_TO PATIENT N:1 WARD (partial for PATIENT if out-patients exist). TREATS DOCTOR M:N PATIENT with relationship attributes Date and Diagnosis.

questions.t: Relationship types of degree higher than two
questions.q: A ternary relationship SUPPLY(Supplier, Part, Project) is replaced by three binary relationships SUPPLIES(Supplier, Part), USES(Project, Part) and CAN_SUPPLY(Supplier, Project). Explain, with an example, why information can be lost.
questions.model: The binaries record pairs only. If s1 supplies p1 to j2 and p2 to j1, the binaries also suggest s1 supplies p1 to j1, which may be false: the ternary fact (s, p, j) cannot be reconstructed from the three pairs.

questions.q: Given EMPLOYEE(eid, name, dept_id, salary) and DEPARTMENT(dept_id, dname), write SQL to list (a) the names of departments whose average salary exceeds 50000 and (b) the employees who earn more than the average salary of their own department.
questions.model:
(a) SELECT d.dname FROM DEPARTMENT d JOIN EMPLOYEE e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id GROUP BY d.dname HAVING AVG(e.salary) > 50000;
(b) SELECT e.name FROM EMPLOYEE e WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(x.salary) FROM EMPLOYEE x WHERE x.dept_id = e.dept_id);

questions.t: Binary Relational Operations: JOIN and DIVISION
questions.q: Using TAKES(sid, cid) and COURSE(cid, title), write a relational algebra expression for the IDs of students who have taken every course, and explain the division operator used.
questions.model: TAKES / pi_cid(COURSE). Division returns the sid values that are paired in TAKES with every cid in pi_cid(COURSE).

questions.q: Map to relations: a weak entity DEPENDENT (partial key name) owned by EMPLOYEE (key ssn), and an M:N relationship WORKS_ON between EMPLOYEE and PROJECT (key pno) with attribute hours. Give primary and foreign keys.
questions.model: DEPENDENT(ssn, name, ...), PK (ssn, name), FK ssn -> EMPLOYEE. WORKS_ON(ssn, pno, hours), PK (ssn, pno), FKs ssn -> EMPLOYEE and pno -> PROJECT.

questions.t: Specifying constraints as Assertion and Trigger
questions.q: Write an SQL trigger on EMPLOYEE(eid, name, salary) that rejects any update reducing an employee's salary, and explain why this rule is better enforced in the database than in each application.
questions.model: CREATE TRIGGER no_salary_cut BEFORE UPDATE OF salary ON EMPLOYEE FOR EACH ROW WHEN (NEW.salary < OLD.salary) BEGIN SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000' SET MESSAGE_TEXT = 'Salary cannot be reduced'; END; (syntax varies by DBMS). The database enforces it for every application and ad hoc update, so the integrity rule cannot be bypassed.

questions.q: R(A, B, C, D, E) has functional dependencies A -> B, B -> C, CD -> E, E -> A. How many candidate keys does R have?
questions.model: D is on no right-hand side, so every key contains D; D alone gives only D. AD, BD, CD and ED each determine all attributes, and no proper subset does: 4 candidate keys.

questions.q: R(Student, Course, Instructor) has FDs {Student, Course} -> Instructor and Instructor -> Course. Show that R is in 3NF but not in BCNF, and give a BCNF decomposition. What is lost?
questions.model: Keys: {Student, Course} and {Student, Instructor}. Instructor -> Course has a non-superkey determinant, violating BCNF, but Course is prime, so 3NF holds. Decompose into (Instructor, Course) and (Student, Instructor): lossless, but {Student, Course} -> Instructor is no longer preserved.

questions.t: General Definitions of Second and Third Normal Forms
questions.q: A relation in which a non-prime attribute depends on only part of a composite candidate key violates which normal form?
questions.model: A partial dependency of a non-prime attribute violates 2NF.

questions.q: R(A, B, C) with F = {A -> B} is decomposed into R1(A, B) and R2(A, C). Is the decomposition lossless? Is it dependency preserving? Justify both.
questions.model: Lossless: R1 intersect R2 = {A}, and A -> B, so A is a key of R1. Dependency preserving: A -> B lies within R1.

questions.q: The ___ property ensures that either all operations of a transaction are reflected in the database or none are, while ___ ensures that the effects of a committed transaction survive system crashes.
questions.model: Atomicity and durability.

questions.q: Is the schedule r1(X), w2(X), w1(X) conflict serializable? Draw the precedence graph and justify your answer.
questions.model: r1(X) before w2(X) gives T1 -> T2; w2(X) before w1(X) gives T2 -> T1. The precedence graph has a cycle, so the schedule is not conflict serializable.

questions.q: Read the assertion and reason about lock Management and choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Basic two-phase locking guarantees conflict-serializable schedules.
questions.reason: Under two-phase locking, a transaction does not release any lock before it has acquired all the locks it needs.
questions.model: Both true and R explains A: the lock point orders the transactions.

questions.q: Explain how checkpoints in the log reduce the work of recovering from a system crash.
questions.model: At a checkpoint the DBMS forces log records and dirty pages to disk and writes a checkpoint record listing active transactions. After a crash, recovery starts from the last checkpoint: committed transactions before it need no redo, and only the log after it (plus active transactions) is scanned.
